messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Rafael Sánchez, a 67-year-old Latin American doctor living in California, has been struggling with the aftermath of his daughter’s life-threatening illness that occurred two years ago. Since then, he has found it increasingly difficult to function both professionally and personally. Dr. Rafael had come to believe that suppressing thoughts about the trauma was the only way to maintain a semblance of normalcy in his life. The traumatic event itself began when Dr. Rafael received an emergency call from the hospital where his daughter was being treated for a severe, undiagnosed illness. The experience was overwhelming and fragmented; he remembers vivid flashes of her frail body hooked up to machines and the sterile smell of antiseptic, but much of what happened remains unclear. He feels like he is only remembering parts of what transpired, and the rest seems missing. This incomplete picture has contributed significantly to his distress. In an effort to avoid thinking about the event, Dr. Rafael keeps himself occupied all the time with work-related tasks, often working late hours at the hospital. However, this constant mental distraction only serves to exacerbate his fragmented memory of the incident. He is unable to find words to describe what happened, and even when he tries to recount it, the story feels disjointed and incoherent. The more Dr. Rafael suppresses thoughts about the trauma, the more hypervigilant he becomes. He remains superalert or watchful at all times, constantly scanning for any signs of illness or danger that could threaten his loved ones. His hyper-awareness has made him jumpy and irritable, especially in clinical settings where reminders of his daughter’s condition are abundant. One day, during a routine patient visit, Dr. Rafael suddenly felt as if the stressful experience were actually happening again. He was struck by an intense flashback that left him feeling physically and emotionally drained. This episode only reinforced his belief that suppressing thoughts about the trauma was crucial to his well-being. Dr. Rafael’s hypervigilance has also led to a growing sense of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. These negative emotions often surface unexpectedly, leaving him on edge and anxious. The more he tries to avoid these feelings by constantly keeping himself busy, the more fragmented his memory becomes. He feels trapped in this cycle, unable to escape the overwhelming thoughts that plague him. Over time, Dr. Rafael has noticed changes in how he interacts with colleagues at work. His frequent absences due to his need for distraction have impacted patient care and strained relationships with his peers. Colleagues who once sought his guidance now avoid engaging with him, sensing his distress. This isolation further deepens his sense of guilt and shame. What finally brought Dr. Rafael to seek help was a realization that his attempts at suppression and constant mental distractions were only making things worse. He was certain that if he continued on this path, the fragmented memories would only worsen, leading to more frequent flashbacks and heightened hypervigilance. What frightened him most was the possibility of losing himself entirely in the trauma, unable to function as a doctor or live a fulfilling life. Dr. Rafael is now seeking help with hopes that he can finally process his daughter’s illness without feeling overwhelmed by guilt and fear. He dreams of finding peace and clarity about what happened, so he can move forward with a sense of wholeness rather than living in fragments.
